29.title: The sun for breakfast
29.hook: baby Hanuman leaps for the sun and comes home with every god's gift; why Hindus ask him for courage
29.howItsDone: Hanuman is one of the most widely worshipped figures in Hinduism; many Hindus visit his temples on Tuesdays or Saturdays, and his childhood stories are told to children as the start of his life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: prasad, the offering that comes back, and a full week with Ganesha. This week belongs to another beloved god, and he starts out hungry.

A baby wakes up hungry. His mother is off gathering fruit. Low on the horizon he sees the rising sun, round and orange-red, exactly like a ripe mango. So he jumps for it. Not a hop: this baby is the son of the wind, and he shoots straight up into the sky, mouth open, reaching for breakfast. The gods watch in alarm. And Indra, king of the gods, lord of storms, does what a nervous king does. He throws his thunderbolt. It strikes the baby on the jaw, and he falls all the way to earth.
screen: `A HUNGRY BABY.` → `THE SUN LOOKS LIKE A MANGO.` → `HE LEAPS.` → `INDRA'S THUNDERBOLT.`

segments.voice: The baby is Hanuman, and the fall gives him his name. Hanu means jaw in Sanskrit. Hanuman: the one with the jaw, the one who was struck. The story is in the Ramayana, the great epic credited to the poet Valmiki, where an old bear, Jambavan, tells it to Hanuman himself. Some tellings say a fruit; many families say a mango. Then comes a shape you've met before. Hanuman's father is Vayu, the wind. When his son falls, Vayu carries him into a cave and stops blowing. The whole world begins to suffocate. So the gods come. They heal the child, and each one gives him a gift: strength, speed, protection from weapons, a long life. Even Indra gives one. The baby knocked out of the sky goes home carrying the gifts of every god. This is why Hindus pray to Hanuman for strength and protection. He isn't only a hero in a story; he's worshipped as a god, with temples of his own, and many devotees visit them on Tuesdays or Saturdays. In Hindi he's often called Bajrangbali, the mighty one with a body like the thunderbolt. Asking Hanuman for courage is asking for strength the gods themselves put in him. Some families keep a small Hanuman in the car for just that reason. And notice: the tradition doesn't mock the baby for reaching too high. It names him for that very day.
screen: `HANU — THE JAW.` · `THE WIND STOPS.` · `EVERY GOD GIVES HIM A GIFT.` · `WHY HINDUS PRAY TO HANUMAN FOR STRENGTH.` · then, large: `HANUMAN HOLDS EVERY GOD'S GIFT.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe slowly, like the wind coming back. Bring to mind something ahead of you that scares you a little: a test, a hard talk, a first day. If you pray, say softly a few times, Om Hanumate Namah, a bow to Hanuman, and ask for his courage. If you don't, picture that baby knocked out of the sky and sent home full of gifts, and let your fear sit beside that picture.
Hanuman. The one with the jaw, named for the thunderbolt that struck him as he leapt for the sun.
Your line: Hanuman holds every god's gift. That's why Hindus ask him for courage. Tomorrow, the strength he forgot he ever had. That's day twenty-nine.

30.title: The forgotten strength
30.hook: cursed to forget his powers until a friend reminds him; who you are can be forgotten, not lost
30.howItsDone: Many Hindus recite the Hanuman Chalisa, a hymn traditionally credited to the poet Tulsidas, for courage in hard times; it retells Hanuman's deeds, including the crossing of the ocean.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Hanuman, the baby who leapt for the sun and came home with a gift from every god. That's why Hindus ask him for courage.

A child with the strength of the wind, and no sense of limits, runs wild through the forest hermitages. Young Hanuman knocks over the sages' water pots and ritual vessels. He tears their bark clothes. Not cruel; just a kid who doesn't know his own size. The sages, patient people, reach the end of their patience. They don't take his strength away. They do something stranger. They curse him to forget it: all that power, and no memory of it, until someone reminds him.
screen: `A CHILD WITH NO LIMITS.` → `THE SAGES' PATIENCE ENDS.` → `HE WILL FORGET.` → `UNTIL SOMEONE REMINDS HIM.`

segments.voice: Years pass. Hanuman grows up gentle, wise and loyal, with no idea what he can do. Now jump ahead. Monkeys and bears stand on the shore, staring at the ocean. Somewhere across it is the island of Lanka, a hundred yojanas away, the text says: an enormous distance. One by one the heroes say how far they could jump. Ten. Twenty. Fifty. Jambavan, the old bear, says ninety, now that he's old. Prince Angada could make the hundred, but isn't sure he could make it back. Hanuman sits apart, quiet. He doesn't even volunteer. Then Jambavan walks over and tells Hanuman his own story. You are the son of the wind. As a baby you leapt for the sun. Every god gave you a gift. Why are you sitting here silent? As he speaks, Hanuman remembers, and he begins to grow, until the others cheer. So the strength was never gone. It was forgotten. Some Hindu teachers read this as a picture of the atman, your tenth word: the true self. In that reading, who you really are can be covered over and forgotten, but never lost, and a teacher's work is to remind you. Jambavan gives no new power. He tells the old story back. Hindus still do this. The Hanuman Chalisa, forty short verses sung in many homes, tells Hanuman's own deeds: the sun, the ocean, the mountain. People sing it when they're afraid, calling on the strength those deeds tell of.

segments.voice: Sit, breathe, and be your own Jambavan for a minute. If you know the Hanuman Chalisa, or another prayer, say a few lines slowly. If you don't, recall a hard thing you got through, or a time you were braver than you expected. Tell yourself plainly, the way the old bear did: that was you. It still is.
Jambavan. The old bear at the ocean's edge who reminds Hanuman of the strength he forgot.
Your line: atman: forgotten, never lost. The true self waits to be remembered. Tomorrow, a meeting in disguise. Day thirty, done.

31.title: Meeting Rama
31.hook: the disguised monkey meets the exiled prince, and a life of bhakti begins
31.carry: bhakti: hanuman's strength kneels to rama
31.howItsDone: Hanuman is honored as the model devotee of Rama; in temples his image often kneels or stands before Rama, Sita and Lakshmana, and devotees chant Rama's name in his honor.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Jambavan, the old bear who told Hanuman his own story back. Forgotten, never lost: who you really are.

A monkey king is hiding on a forest mountain. Sugriva has been driven from his kingdom by his own brother, and he's scared of everyone. Then two men come walking up the valley: tall, dressed like hermits in bark, but carrying bows. Assassins, he thinks, sent by his brother. So he sends his most trusted adviser to find out. Hanuman. And Hanuman goes in disguise too, as a wandering holy man. He bows to the strangers and asks polite, careful questions. Two sides, both hiding who they are, trying to read each other.
screen: `A KING IN HIDING.` → `TWO ARMED HERMITS.` → `HANUMAN IN DISGUISE.`

segments.voice: The two men are Rama, a prince in exile, and his brother Lakshmana. Rama's wife, Sita, has been taken; you'll hear the whole story from its start in a few days. Watch what happens when Hanuman speaks. In Valmiki's Ramayana, Rama turns to his brother and says, more or less: listen to him. Nobody talks like this without deep study. Not one word out of place, not too long, not too rushed. Someone who speaks like this could win over an enemy with a raised sword. Rama knows Hanuman by how he talks, before he knows who he is. And Hanuman knows Rama. He drops the disguise, shows his true form, lifts both brothers onto his shoulders and carries them up the mountain to his king. From here on, his life is devotion to Rama. That's bhakti, your sixteenth word, with a face. And here's why it matters to Hindus. Hanuman is the strongest one in the story, and he spends that strength serving. In temples his image often kneels before Rama, Sita and Lakshmana. Near the end of the epic, he asks for one thing: to live on earth as long as Rama's story is told. So at many Ramayana readings, devotees set out a seat for him, trusting that wherever Rama's story is told, Hanuman comes to listen. Strength that kneels. That's bhakti.

32.title: The leap
32.hook: the ocean to Lanka; the mountain that offers rest; no rest till Rama's work is done
32.carry: no rest till rama's work is done
32.howItsDone: Some Hindus read or recite the Sundara Kanda, the Ramayana's book of Hanuman's journey, as a devotional practice, sometimes in full over a day or across several days, especially in difficult times.

segments.voice: Yesterday: meeting Rama. Two disguises, and a monkey who gave his whole strength to a prince. Bhakti: strength that kneels.

Hanuman climbs a mountain on the shore and grows huge. He presses down so hard that the rocks crack and the trees shake loose their flowers. Then he jumps. The text makes a spectacle of it: blossoms pulled along behind him, his shadow racing over the waves like a ship. He's flying to Lanka to find Sita. Halfway across, a mountain named Mainaka rises out of the sea, and speaks. You're doing a great thing for a good cause. Rest on me. Eat some fruit. A kind offer, from a real mountain, right there.
screen: `HE CRACKS THE MOUNTAIN.` → `HE JUMPS.` → `A MOUNTAIN RISES: REST ON ME.`

segments.voice: Hanuman thanks the mountain. He touches it politely with his hand and says: I've made a promise; I can't stop. And he flies on. Centuries later the poet Tulsidas gave him a line here that Hindi speakers still quote: without finishing Rama's work, where is rest for me? The next test comes straight after. The gods send Surasa, mother of serpents, to see what he's made of. She rises from the water, mouth open: nobody passes me without going in. Hanuman grows bigger. She opens wider. Bigger. Wider. Then he shrinks to the size of a thumb, darts into her mouth and straight back out, and bows. I went in. Now let me go. Surasa laughs and blesses him. A third test follows, Simhika, a creature who grabs shadows, and he gets past her too. Now remember what he said before he jumped. Valmiki has him say he'll fly to Lanka like an arrow shot by Rama. That's the secret of the leap. It isn't Hanuman's errand. It's Rama's work, and Rama's work carries him. This whole journey is the Sundara Kanda, the beautiful book, the fifth book of the Ramayana, Hanuman's book. Many Hindu families read it whole in hard times or before a big step, because it's the book where a devotee crosses what no one can cross, doing God's work. No rest till Rama's work is done.

33.title: Finding Sita
33.hook: the ashoka grove; Rama's story sung softly from a tree; the ring
33.howItsDone: The scene of Hanuman giving Rama's ring to Sita in the ashoka grove is often painted and performed, and it's a high point when devotees recite the Sundara Kanda.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the leap. A mountain thanked and passed, and a monkey flying like Rama's arrow. No rest till Rama's work is done.
screen: `NO REST TILL RAMA'S WORK IS DONE.`

segments.voice: Lanka at night: a city of gold, full of music, feasting and guards. Hanuman shrinks to the size of a cat and searches, palace after palace, room after room. He sees the demon king Ravana's wives asleep, and for a moment wonders if one is Sita. Then he stops himself. No. Sita would never sleep peacefully here. He almost gives up. Then, at the city's edge, a grove of ashoka trees. Under one tree, guarded by fierce women, sits a woman in a single worn cloth, thin from grief, refusing everything she's offered. He climbs into the branches above her and waits.
screen: `A CITY OF GOLD, AT NIGHT.` → `NOT HER. NOT HERE.` → `A GARDEN OF ASHOKA TREES.` → `A WOMAN UNDER A TREE.`

segments.voice: Hanuman has a problem. If a giant monkey drops out of a tree in the enemy's city and says Rama sent me, she'll scream, and he'll be caught. So he does something gentle. Hidden in the leaves, he softly tells Rama's story, the one she knows best. Sita looks up. He comes down, bows, and gives her proof of who he is: Rama's ring. She holds it, the text says, with joy, as though she'd found her husband again. Then Hanuman offers: climb on my back, and I'll carry you across the ocean tonight. But in Valmiki, Sita says no. She won't willingly touch any man but her husband, and she wants Rama to come himself and end this properly. She gives Hanuman a jewel from her hair, and a small private story only Rama would know. Ring in, jewel out. Now look at how Hanuman first reached her. Not with strength. With Rama's story, sung softly from a tree. Hearing it, she knew a friend was near. Hindu teachers count this as devotion: in a well-known list of nine ways of bhakti, the first is shravana, simply hearing God's story. That's why families sit through long Ramayana readings, and grandparents tell these stories at bedtime. The story is how hope gets into a guarded place. Hearing God's story is devotion.

34.title: The burning tail
34.hook: caught and set on fire to shame him, Hanuman burns Lanka; the fire comes home to the one who lit it
34.carry: karma: the fire you light comes home
34.howItsDone: The burning of Lanka is a favorite scene in Ramlila performances across North India, and devotees recite it as part of the Sundara Kanda.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rama's story sung from a tree, a ring in, a jewel out, and Sita's quiet no. Hearing God's story is devotion.

The job is done. He's found Sita and has her jewel. He could slip away tonight and no one in Lanka would know. Instead, Hanuman wants to see the enemy up close, so he does something loud. He tears up the royal garden, tree by tree, and fights off wave after wave of warriors. Finally Ravana's son, Indrajit, binds him with a divine weapon. Hanuman could break free. He lets himself be dragged into the court of the ten-headed king. He wanted to be caught: it was the only way in the front door.
screen: `THE JOB IS DONE.` → `HE TEARS UP THE GARDEN.` → `HE LETS THEM CATCH HIM.`

segments.voice: Before Ravana, Hanuman speaks plainly: give Sita back, make peace with Rama. Ravana, furious, orders him killed. His younger brother, Vibhishana, objects: you don't kill a messenger; that's not how kings behave. Remember Vibhishana; he matters later. So Ravana picks a humiliation instead. A monkey's pride is his tail, he says. Burn it. The guards wrap the tail in rags, soak it in oil, set it alight, and parade Hanuman through the streets to laughter. Then he shrinks, slips his ropes, grows huge again and leaps onto the rooftops. Tail blazing, he jumps from palace to palace, and the golden city goes up in flames. When Sita hears they've set his tail on fire, she prays to Agni, god of fire, that it be cool for him. Mid-leap, Hanuman notices it isn't hurting him at all. Then panic: what if I've burned the garden where she is? He rushes back. She's safe. Now notice who lit the fire. Ravana chose it, to shame a messenger. By nightfall it was his own city burning. Many teachers read this as karma, your seventh word: every action bears fruit, and the fruit comes back to the one who acted. No one had to punish Ravana; his own act ripened on his own roofs, and the woman he wronged, praying, was the one place it couldn't touch. So the lesson isn't burn things down. It's in Ravana's hands. The fire you light comes home.
screen: `GIVE HER BACK.` · `THEY SET THE TAIL ALIGHT.` · `SITA PRAYS: BE COOL FOR HIM.` · `RAVANA'S FIRE, RAVANA'S CITY.` · then, large: `KARMA: THE FIRE YOU LIGHT COMES HOME.`

segments.voice: Sit and breathe. Bring to mind something said or done to shame you, and notice the pull to throw it back. Don't. Picture handing that fire over, the way Sita prayed to Agni, and asking that it burn no one, including you. If you pray, say it to God in your own words. If you don't, breathe out slowly, and set it down.
Lanka. Ravana's golden island city, set ablaze by the tail they lit to shame Hanuman.

35.title: The mountain of herbs
35.hook: can't tell which herb, so he brings the whole mountain; sankat mochan and seva
35.howItsDone: Many Hindus call on Hanuman as Sankat Mochan in times of trouble, visiting his temples, including the Sankat Mochan temple in Varanasi, and reciting the Hanuman Chalisa.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lanka ablaze, and a fire that came home to the one who lit it. Karma. Today, a picture of Hanuman you may have seen: a monkey flying, holding a mountain.
screen: `KARMA: THE FIRE YOU LIGHT COMES HOME.`

segments.voice: Night on the battlefield, later in the story, in the war for Lanka. Rama's brother Lakshmana lies struck down by a terrible weapon, barely breathing. The camp's healer says there's one hope: certain herbs that grow on a mountain in the Himalayas, far to the north. Bring them before sunrise, and he lives. It's a vast distance, and only one of them could cover it that fast. Hanuman goes. He crosses the land in the dark, finds the mountain, lands, and stops. There are plants everywhere, glowing in the night. He doesn't know which ones are the herbs. And the sun will not wait.

So he picks up the whole mountain. He tears off the peak, balances it on one hand, and flies it back to the battlefield. The healer finds the herbs, and Lakshmana lives. That image, Hanuman in the sky with a mountain on his palm, turns up on calendars, temple walls and truck doors. The race against sunrise comes from later tellings. Today's word is a name people call him by. Sankat mochan. Sankat means trouble, a crisis, a tight spot. Mochan means release, setting free. The one who frees you from trouble. In Varanasi there's a great temple by that name, and people who are frightened, sick, broke or grieving go and stand before him. Look at his choice. He didn't know exactly what was needed, and he didn't wait until he did. He brought everything. That's seva, your fifteenth word, at full size: service that doesn't do the minimum. Now look back at the week. A baby who reached for the sun and came home with every god's gift. A strength forgotten, never lost. A meeting that began a life of bhakti. A leap made for Rama's work. A story sung softly from a tree. A fire that came home to the one who lit it. And a whole mountain, because one leaf might have been the wrong one. Tomorrow, the Ramayana begins, from the very start.
screen: `HE LIFTS THE WHOLE PEAK.` · `SANKAT MOCHAN — FREER FROM TROUBLE.` · `SEVA AT FULL SIZE.` · `A WEEK WITH HANUMAN.` · then, large: `SEVA: BRING THE WHOLE MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: A seva review: look back over the last week, at where you served someone, with a favor, a meal, time or attention, and where you did the minimum when you could have brought more. No guilt; this isn't a scoreboard. Then hold one person in trouble right now in mind. If you pray, say Hanuman's name for them, the way people call on Sankat Mochan. Then ask what bringing the whole mountain would look like for them.
Sankat mochan. The one who frees from trouble: Hanuman, who flew a mountain through the night so a friend would live.
